INTERNAL ONLY (Redwood Inference) — Speaker notes for the Standard Demo v1
Last updated: 2025-02-14 (Soojin). Please comment inline rather than forking.


0) Purpose + what this doc is
- This is the word-for-word-ish narration + click-path + “if asked…” sidebars for running the standard demo tenant live.
- This is designed to work for three common personas:
  1) Platform Eng / Infra (cares about reliability, SLOs, deploy modes, guardrails)
  2) ML Eng / Applied (cares about quality, determinism, evals, model choice, throughput)
  3) Security / Compliance (cares about isolation, retention, audit logs, KMS, RBAC/SSO)
- If you’re short on time, jump to Section 6 “2-minute Hosted mini-demo” or Section 7 “12-minute core flow.”


1) Roles during the call (recommended)
- Driver (SE): runs Console + terminal. Keep your cursor intentional. Don’t freestyle.
- Narrator (AE/SE): owns storyline, keeps time, handles most questions.
- Optional (PM/Eng): silent backup. Only speaks when prompted.

Suggested opening (narrator):
“Just to keep this tight: I’ll narrate and keep time, and Markus will drive the Console and the API calls. Please interrupt with questions—we’ll either answer inline or we’ll park it and come back at the end.”


2) Pre-demo checklist (do this 20–30 min before)
- Confirm demo tenant is green:
  - Console → Demo Tenant → Dashboards → ‘Demo Tenant Health (v1)’
  - Verify last 15m: 5xx < 0.5%, p95 latency within the ‘green band’ notes on the dashboard.
- Confirm model pins are correct for scenarios:
  - Console → Routes → (route group) ‘standard-demo’ → check primary + fallback are pinned to the expected versions.
- Confirm quotas/rate limits won’t trip during live:
  - Console → Settings → Quotas & Rate Limits → ensure you’re on the “Demo Safe” policy.
- Confirm seeded artifacts exist:
  - Console → Observe → Saved Views: “Streaming Chat Trace (seed)”, “Tool Call Trace (seed)”, “Fallback Event Trace (seed)”.
- Open your tabs ahead of time (minimize tab switching):
  1) Console: Routes
  2) Console: Dashboards
  3) Console: Traces (Observe)
  4) Terminal (curl scripts) OR Notebook
  5) (Optional) Security FAQ (Confluence) in a separate window

Driver note: do NOT show raw tenant IDs, internal cluster names, or any access tokens. If the Console has an ‘internal details’ toggle, keep it OFF.


3) Ground rules for the demo (say this out loud)
Suggested phrasing:
“A quick framing: in a live demo, the only thing that’s truly deterministic is what we control. So we use known-good prompts and we’ll show you the instrumentation and controls around latency/cost/reliability. Output can still vary slightly—that’s normal for generative models—and we’ll call out where that matters.”

If they’re skeptical about nondeterminism:
“We can run with temperature=0 for more stable behavior, but the real value is that we can detect regressions and roll forward/back safely. We’ll show that.”


4) Default agenda (30 min)
- 0–3 min: What Redwood is + what you’ll see
- 3–12 min: Live API call (streaming) + latency/cost visibility
- 12–20 min: Reliability: routing + fallback + guardrails
- 20–26 min: Observability: traces, error analysis, cost breakdown
- 26–30 min: Deployment modes: Hosted → Dedicated → Private mapping to their constraints

Short agenda (12–15 min): skip deep observability; only show 1 dashboard + 1 trace.


5) Opening: positioning (0:00–2:30)
Narrator script:
“Redwood Inference is an inference platform focused on serving economics: consistent latency, predictable cost, and reliability—across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Today we’ll do three things live:
(1) make real API calls with streaming,
(2) show the knobs that move cost/latency without hand-waving,
and (3) show reliability behaviors—like fallbacks—so your product doesn’t go down when capacity is constrained or an upstream model is degraded.”

Transition line:
“I’ll start with a simple ‘hello world’ that’s actually production-shaped: streaming chat with observability.”


6) 2-minute Hosted mini-demo (for time-crunched calls)
Use when: inbound, early-stage, or “we just need to see it work.”
Goal: show streaming + one cost/latency panel.

Driver steps:
A) Terminal: run streaming chat
- If using curl scripts from redwood-examples:
  - local: `./demo/streaming_chat.sh` (confirm your script name; don’t improvise on the call)
- If using raw curl (template; do not paste tokens on-screen):
  - Endpoint: POST /v1/chat/completions with stream=true
  - Model route: `demo-chat-primary`

Narrator (while streaming):
“Two things to watch: first, it’s token streaming—so your app can start rendering immediately. Second, everything you’re seeing is traceable end-to-end in the Console, down to token-level timing and cost.”

B) Console click-path: show the request in traces
- Console → Observe → Traces
- Filter: Route = demo-chat-primary (or saved view “Streaming Chat Trace (seed)”)
- Click most recent trace

Narrator:
“This is the exact request we just made. You can see latency breakdown, token counts, and the model version actually served. The point is: you’re not guessing where time and money go.”

C) Dashboard (one panel)
- Console → Dashboards → “Demo Tenant Cost & Latency (v1)”
- Call out p50/p95 + tokens/sec panel

Close:
“If this looks directionally right, the next step is we map one of your endpoints onto a route with an SLO and a cost target, and run a small eval set so you can make an informed choice on model + serving profile.”


7) 12-minute core flow (recommended default for first meeting)

7.1 Streaming chat + latency/cost framing (2:30–6:00)
Narrator setup phrase:
“Let’s assume a common workload: a customer-support assistant that needs low perceived latency and predictable spend.”

Driver steps:
1) Terminal: run “Scenario 1 — Streaming Chat”
2) Show the stream for 10–15 seconds, then stop scrolling.

Narrator (exact phrasing, keep it tight):
“What Redwood controls is the serving layer: batching, caching, routing, and fallbacks. You keep control over prompts and models. We make the economics measurable.”

Console click-path (immediately after):
- Console → Observe → Traces → open latest trace
- Point to:
  - Total latency + time-to-first-token
  - Total tokens in/out
  - Any caching indicator (if enabled)

If asked: “Is this your model?”
Answer:
“We support a curated catalog plus customer-provided models depending on deployment mode. For the demo we use pinned, known-good versions so the story stays stable. In a POC we’d validate the exact model(s) you care about.”


7.2 Cost controls + what levers exist (6:00–8:30)
Narrator (do NOT quote exact $ unless approved):
“Cost is usually the combination of (a) how many tokens you generate, (b) what hardware profile you’re on, and (c) how efficiently you can serve many requests—batching and caching without breaking latency.”

Driver click-path:
- Console → Routes
- Open route group: “standard-demo”
- Open route: “demo-chat-primary”
- Show: serving profile (batching on/off), cache policy, max output tokens guardrail

Narrator:
“These are the practical guardrails: output caps, timeouts, and policies that prevent runaway spend. And these settings are versioned with the route so you can roll them forward safely.”

If asked: “Do you do prompt caching?”
Answer:
“Yes. Prefix/KV caching where it makes sense, with controls so you can choose what’s cacheable. In regulated contexts, we can scope caching to an isolated environment or disable it entirely.”


7.3 Reliability: routing + fallback (8:30–11:30)
Narrator setup phrase:
“This is where a lot of teams get burned in production: a model endpoint degrades, a region gets hot, or you hit a capacity cliff. Redwood lets you define what ‘graceful degradation’ means for your app.”

Driver: show the routing policy first (before triggering anything)
- Console → Routes → route: “demo-chat-primary”
- Click tab: Routing / Fallback (label varies; use whatever Console says)
- Show:
  - Primary target (Model A, version pinned)
  - Fallback target (Model B or quantized variant)
  - Trigger conditions (example: error rate threshold, p95 latency threshold, capacity unavailable)

Narrator (exact phrasing):
“We’re not claiming fallbacks solve everything. We’re saying you get to define an explicit policy, and we make the behavior observable, testable, and reversible.”

Driver: run the canned “fallback trigger” scenario (do not hack it live)
- Terminal script: “Scenario 3 — Fallback Routing (canned)”
- Expected: request is served by fallback target; trace shows fallback event

Console click-path to prove it:
- Console → Observe → Traces
- Open latest trace
- Show field: ‘served_by’ or ‘target’ includes fallback model/version
- Show ‘policy decision’ / ‘fallback reason’ panel (if present)

If the fallback doesn’t trigger (Plan B):
- Don’t retry more than once.
- Say:
  “Rather than burn time trying to reproduce a transient condition, I’ll show you the saved trace from our regression check that demonstrates the exact behavior.”
- Console → Observe → Saved Views → “Fallback Event Trace (seed)”

If asked: “Does this work across regions?”
Answer:
“Yes—routing policies can incorporate region and tier. For EMEA data residency needs, we can constrain routing to EU regions only, and still have fallbacks within that boundary.”


7.4 Observability: dashboards + error analysis (11:30–14:00)
Narrator:
“The real difference between a demo and production is: can you debug and control this when it’s 2 a.m.? Here’s what we provide out of the box.”

Driver click-path:
- Console → Dashboards → “Demo Tenant Health (v1)”
- Scroll intentionally to panels:
  - Request rate / throughput
  - Error rate (4xx vs 5xx)
  - Latency p50/p95
  - Token cost breakdown (if present)

Then:
- Console → Observe → Error Analysis (or Traces filtered by status)
- Filter: status >= 500 OR route = demo-chat-primary

Narrator:
“You can slice by route, model version, and timeframe, and you can export traces to your stack if you want—Datadog/Splunk/SIEM depending on deployment.”


8) Persona branches (choose one, don’t do all)

8.1 Platform Eng branch (reliability + operability)
Use when: they ask about SLAs, oncall, SLOs, incident modes.

Narrator:
“You’re probably thinking: what’s the failure mode and who owns it? Our goal is to make inference behave like a well-run service: clear SLOs, clear throttling behavior, and policies for degradation instead of chaos.”

Driver focus:
- Routes → quotas/rate limits policy view
- Show how throttles are surfaced (429s) + headers (if available)

If asked: “Can we reserve capacity?”
Answer:
“Yes—Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput and isolation. Same API surface; different control plane and operational model.”


8.2 ML Eng branch (quality + evals + versioning)
Use when: they push on output quality, regression, model choice.

Narrator:
“We treat model + serving profile as a versioned release. The way you avoid ‘it got worse overnight’ is pinning + evals + canaries.”

Driver click-path:
- Console → Rollouts (or Model Lifecycle / Releases)
- Show:
  - pinned model version on the route
  - a canary knob (if enabled in demo tenant)
  - rollback history (if visible)

If asked: “Do you support structured output / tool calling?”
Answer:
“Yes. We’ll show a quick tool call scenario that returns JSON with schema validation. In production, you’d back it with an eval set so you can measure adherence.”

Optional add-on (only if time):
- Run “Scenario 2 — Tool Calling / Structured Output”
- Show trace with tool call payload + validation result


8.3 Security branch (isolation + retention + audit logs)
Use when: security is present, or procurement vibe.

Narrator (keep it factual, no improvising certifications):
“On security: for the demo tenant specifically, it’s sanitized—no customer data, restricted access, and logging configured to be safe for live calls. For real deployments, the controls depend on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.”

If asked: “Are prompts stored? What’s retention?”
Answer (safe phrasing):
“By default we log what we need to operate the service and debug issues, and we have configurable retention and redaction controls. For customers with stricter requirements, Private deployments support customer-managed retention policies and tighter logging boundaries. We can go through the exact configuration that fits your policy.”

If asked: “SSO/SAML/RBAC?”
Answer:
“Yes—Console access supports SSO and RBAC. For the demo tenant, access is restricted to approved Redwood users and we can show you the control points at a high level without exposing internal identities.”

If asked: “Encryption / KMS?”
Answer:
“Data in transit is encrypted. At rest encryption is standard, and for Private deployments we support customer-managed keys via your KMS/HSM integrations. The exact details are in the security package; we can share under NDA or via your security review process.”

If asked: “Audit logs / SIEM?”
Answer:
“Yes—audit logs are available for control plane actions, and we can integrate with SIEM workflows depending on deployment mode. If it helps, we can walk through what events are captured (route changes, access, key config changes) and how they’re exported.”

Driver (do NOT dig into internal logs on-screen):
- If asked to “show audit logs” and the demo tenant UI supports it safely:
  - Console → Security / Audit Logs → filter by “Route updated” (pre-seeded event)
- If not supported visibly in demo tenant:
  - Say:
    “We have a security FAQ we can send immediately after this call with exact retention and audit log details, and we can do a security-only follow-up where we go deeper.”


9) Handling common objections (quick responses)

Objection: “We can just run vLLM ourselves.”
Response:
“You can, and many teams start there. Where it gets hard is operating it like a product: routing policies, fallbacks, cost controls, observability, rollouts, and doing it across hosted/dedicated/private with the same interface. We try to remove that operational tax.”

Objection: “Your latency numbers might not match ours.”
Response:
“Totally fair. That’s why we prefer to measure on your prompts and traffic shape. What we’re demonstrating today is the control surface and the ability to see and tune the contributing factors.”

Objection: “Model output changes will break our app.”
Response:
“That’s exactly why we push pinning and canaries. You can keep a stable production route and roll forward with eval gates. And if a release regresses, rollback is a policy action, not an incident.”

Objection: “I don’t want a surprise bill / throttling.”
Response:
“Two parts: guardrails (caps/timeouts/quotas) and visibility (token-level cost, route-level spend). And if you need predictability beyond that, Dedicated gives reserved capacity with contract terms.”


10) Plan B / failure modes (read this before every live demo)
- Streaming disconnects:
  - Say: “We’ve seen occasional client-side streaming disconnects depending on network conditions. The request still completes server-side; I’ll pull the trace to show the full completion.”
  - Then go to Console → Observe → Traces → open the request.
- Console feels slow / dashboard lag:
  - Switch to Saved Views in Observe (seeded) rather than live filtering.
  - Do not wait in silence. Narrate: “I’m going to use a saved view so we don’t waste your time on UI latency.”
- Model output is weird:
  - Do not argue with the model.
  - Say: “That’s a good example of why we recommend eval-driven rollouts. For the demo, we’ll switch to the pinned canned output trace so we can focus on the operational controls.”


11) Closing + next steps (last 2–3 min)
Narrator close:
“What we showed is: production-shaped inference with measurable latency/cost, explicit reliability policies, and the observability to debug it quickly. The usual next step is a short evaluation:
- you give us 20–50 representative prompts and expected behaviors,
- we deploy into Hosted or Dedicated depending on constraints,
- and we review results together with cost/latency/quality tradeoffs.”

If security is present:
“We can run the technical eval in parallel with a lightweight security review. We’ll send the security FAQ right after this call and line up a deeper session if needed.”

Hard ask (AE-friendly):
“Would it be reasonable to schedule a 45-minute follow-up where we map one of your endpoints to a route policy and define what ‘good’ means—latency target, cost target, and fallback behavior?”


Appendix A — Click-path cheat sheet (driver)
- Routes:
  Console → Routes → standard-demo → demo-chat-primary
- Routing/fallback:
  Console → Routes → demo-chat-primary → Routing / Fallback
- Traces:
  Console → Observe → Traces → filter by Route
- Saved views:
  Console → Observe → Saved Views → (Streaming Chat Trace / Fallback Event Trace / Tool Call Trace)
- Dashboards:
  Console → Dashboards → Demo Tenant Health (v1)
  Console → Dashboards → Demo Tenant Cost & Latency (v1)
- Quotas:
  Console → Settings → Quotas & Rate Limits → Demo Safe policy


Appendix B — Phrases that tested well in dry runs (use these)
- “Serving economics: latency, cost, reliability—measurable and controllable.”
- “Graceful degradation is a policy decision, not an incident.”
- “Pinned versions + evals + canaries prevent ‘it got worse overnight’.”
- “We’re not asking you to trust a benchmark slide; we’re giving you the instrumentation to measure on your workload.”


Appendix C — Don’ts (please)
- Don’t quote per-token prices or exact latency numbers unless you’re using the approved ranges from PMM.
- Don’t open internal admin views, cluster details, or any screen with secrets.
- Don’t run ad-hoc prompts that could generate unsafe content. Stay on the canned prompts.
- Don’t debug live for more than ~60 seconds. Switch to Plan B.
